First big international trip · ~14 days · from Florida

Iceland, or Spain + Italy, or Italy + Greece?

Three researched routes, priced leg by leg — flights in cash and Chase points kept separate, route maps drawn out, and an honest read on what each one does badly.

Home airports: Tampa (TPA) · Orlando (MCO) Economy Researched Nov 3, 2026 Prices are dated snapshots, not quotes — re-check before booking Nothing booked, held, or transferred

The recommendation

Spain + Italy, lean version — Madrid → Barcelona → Rome → Florence — if this is a spring or fall trip and you want the classic first Europe experience. It's the only option where almost every move is a fast train from city center to city center, it has the clearest Chase points play (Iberia Avios to Madrid), and it carries the least weather risk.

Italy + Greece wins instead if the sea is the point — museums first, then actually slowing down on an island. It costs you one full travel day and a ferry-or-flight dependency to get it.

Iceland is a different trip, not a worse one: the shortest flight from Florida, the least jet lag, zero language friction — and the highest daily cost, real weather risk, and almost no cities or food culture. It wins if nature and driving are the priority and the month is May–September. Don't bolt a full second country onto a full Ring Road in 14 days; if Iceland calls, use Icelandair's stopover and give the second country one city, done properly.

This call is conditional until you answer the questions at the bottom of this tab — especially the month. Season changes the answer more than country preference does.

Daily costs are published guide ranges (solo, mid-range, excluding the transatlantic flight); sources disagree on exact numbers but agree on the order: Iceland most expensive, Spain cheapest of the Mediterranean three. Full sourcing in each tab.

The real question: Spain or Greece next to Italy?

Both combos contain Italy, so the swap isn't country-for-country — it changes what the second half of the trip does.

With Spain, the second half is…

  • More cities, more food. Tapas and market culture, late dinners (9–10:30 pm is normal), Gaudí, the Prado.
  • Rail the whole way. Madrid→Barcelona 2h30 by high-speed train; Italy's spine is rail too. One short flight (Barcelona→Rome) is the only air leg.
  • Predictable. The main risk is summer heat, not cancelled transport.
  • Weak on beaches unless you deliberately add a coast stop.
  • Lower friction: trains, cities, English widely usable in tourist areas.

With Greece, the second half is…

  • Sea, light, and a slowdown after a museum-heavy Italy half. The rhythm is better — if you protect it.
  • Flights and ferries, not trains. "Do not think trains in Greece" is the forum line — it's car, bus, and ferry, plus a backtrack through Athens to get home.
  • Weather-dependent. Summer meltemi winds can cancel Cyclades ferries; winter sailings thin out sharply.
  • Athens ≠ Rome. A world-class ancient core, but it doesn't replace Rome + Florence as a museum city. Greece dilutes Italy's art depth.
  • Cheaper day-to-day than Italy outside Santorini/Mykonos peak — but island transfers add cost back.
Plainly: want the most classic sights per day with the least that can go wrong → Spain + Italy. Want to come home rested, with a real beach/island payoff → Italy + Greece, one island only, fly (don't ferry) to Santorini, and keep a buffer night in Athens before the flight home. Want beaches and cities and low stress in 14 days → neither combo is ideal; that's the case for Iceland + one stopover city, or one country done well.

What would change the recommendation

  • Solo, or with Arwen? Iceland's car-vs-tour math flips on this — forums note a rental car beats tour prices for a group, while a solo traveler often does better on tours. It also doubles the points math.
  • Which month? The single biggest variable. December kills the Iceland road trip and the Greek islands; August punishes all three Mediterranean cities. September flatters everything.
  • Beach/sea or cities/food/history — if you had to cut one, which goes? That's the Spain-vs-Greece tiebreaker.
  • Driving comfort? Iceland is a rental-car trip, full stop. Wind and gravel are part of it. And seasickness — a 5-hour fast ferry is not a small ask.
  • Budget band: is a ~$250–350/day Iceland realistic, or does the Mediterranean band (~$120–200/day) matter more?
  • Is Santorini specifically the dream, or would a calmer, cheaper island (Naxos, Paros) do if it saves money and crowds?

Two things already in motion, for context: the Vietnam trip (Apr 9–22, 2027) gets its own separate page, and the Switzerland Travelzoo package decision is due Wed Nov 4 — this Europe debate doesn't replace either.

The route: full Ring Road, counter-clockwise

Route 1 circles the whole country. Forums are blunt about the minimum: under 10 days is a squeeze, 12 feels rushed, 14 does it justice. A 7-day version is a different, smaller trip — Golden Circle + South Coast only.

Map unavailable — the numbered stop list below is the route, in order.

    Day by day (14 days)

    1. Day 1
      Arrive Keflavík → ReykjavíkLand, pick up the car, easy afternoon. Blue Lagoon is near the airport if you want the soak on arrival day — book ahead, capacity is limited.
    2. Day 2
      Golden CircleÞingvellir, Geysir, Gullfoss — the greatest-hits loop, back to Reykjavík or stay out on the circle.
    3. Days 3–4
      South Coast → Vík (2 nights)Seljalandsfoss and Skógafoss waterfalls, black-sand Reynisfjara beach. Two nights here instead of one is what keeps the pace sane.
    4. Day 5
      Höfn / JökulsárlónGlacier lagoon with floating icebergs and Diamond Beach — the drive east is the show.
    5. Day 6
      East Fjords → EgilsstaðirQuiet fjord villages, reindeer country, the least-crowded stretch of the ring.
    6. Days 7–8
      Mývatn areaVolcanic craters, lava fields, geothermal baths — the north's weird-geology base (near Akureyri).
    7. Days 9–10
      Akureyri (2 nights)Iceland's second town: whale watching from nearby Húsavík, a real bed-and-restaurants pause mid-ring.
    8. Day 11
      West toward SnæfellsnesThe long scenic transfer day across the north-west.
    9. Day 12
      Snæfellsnes Peninsula"Iceland in miniature" — glacier, lava beaches, Kirkjufell mountain.
    10. Day 13
      Back to ReykjavíkBuffer day. This is deliberate: Icelandic weather eats itineraries, and this day is the shock absorber.
    11. Day 14
      Fly home from KeflavíkShort drive to the airport; the nonstop gets you back to Orlando same day.

    Flights — cash and points, kept separate

    cash Orlando → Keflavík

    • Nonstop on Icelandair, ~7h 25m — the shortest long-haul of any option here, and the only verified nonstop gateway pairing besides Madrid.
    • KAYAK snapshots found Nov 3 conflict: cheapest nonstop $658, typical $683–$932; a separate snapshot showed cheapest round-trip $554, average $743. Read that as a $550–$950 band to re-check for your dates, not a quote.
    • Tampa: no TPA nonstop to Iceland was verified in this research. Plan on driving to MCO unless a live check proves otherwise.

    points The Chase problem

    • There is no direct Chase → Icelandair transfer. Icelandair's Saga Club doesn't take the major US transferable currencies (per award-tool sources — verify before relying on it).
    • The forum-adjacent workarounds: JetBlue TrueBlue (a Chase 1:1 partner) prices Icelandair economy from the US East Coast — one tool figure was Boston–Keflavík from 17,000 pts + ~$102 one-way. That's an article/tool lead, not forum-verified and not priced from Florida — check JetBlue.com for your dates.
    • Virgin Atlantic (also Chase 1:1) for Delta's seasonal Reykjavík nonstops was quoted in articles at 30,000–50,000 pts round-trip economy vs. Delta's dynamic pricing. Article-only; verify live.
    • No FlyerTalk thread found on booking Icelandair with Chase points from TPA/MCO specifically — this is the weakest points option of the three trips.

    Getting around — there is no train, and that's the point

    Rental car the default

    Public transport outside Reykjavík is too thin for a Ring Road — forums treat the car as close to mandatory. Iceland drives on the right, like the US, and posters call summer driving "super easy" outside the capital (roundabouts are the main adjustment). Take all the insurance — gravel, sand, and ash damage is a known Iceland-specific risk — and check safetravel.is and vedur.is before every driving day. Strong winds can close highways; gas stations get sparse in the east and north.

    Guided tours / buses

    Day tours cover Golden Circle and the South Coast from Reykjavík well, and multi-day tours run the ring. The forum math: for a group, a car is often cheaper than per-person tour fares and gets you to sights before the tour buses; for a solo traveler, tours can be cheaper and save the driving fatigue. Tours also solve the winter problem — a guide drives, you don't.

    Rideshare / taxi

    No Uber-style coverage to plan a trip around — taxis exist in Reykjavík, and the airport is ~45 min from the city (Flybus is the standard transfer). Outside the capital, it's your car or a tour. Nothing like Vietnam's Grab here.

    The +1 country version: stopover, not a second trip

    Icelandair's stopover program is described across guides as up to 7 nights in Iceland at no extra airfare on a North America–Europe ticket (hotels and tours in Iceland are extra; terms vary by fare class — verify on icelandair.com for your dates). The only sensible 14-day shape:

    • 3–4 nights Iceland: Reykjavík, Golden Circle, South Coast to Vík. A taste — not the Ring Road.
    • 8–9 nights one European city (London, Paris, Amsterdam, or Copenhagen are the natural stopover pairings) — one base, day trips, no hotel-hopping.
    • Fly home from that city. Do not try full Ring Road + a full second country in 14 days — that's three trips wearing a trench coat.

    What Iceland does badly

    • Cost. Every source agrees it's Europe's most expensive of these four — published 2026 mid-range bands run roughly $250–$350/day (guides conflict; direction doesn't). A Mediterranean daily budget will not transfer.
    • Winter. December–January means 4–5 hours of daylight and frequent storms. Aurora season (Sep–Mar) is real, but a winter Ring Road needs a guided plan and buffer days, not a rental-car itinerary.
    • It's one note: landscape. Cities, museums, food variety, warmth, and beaches are not this trip. September is the best first-visit compromise: ~13 hrs daylight mid-month, roads open, nights dark enough for aurora, crowds down.
    • Volcanic activity near Grindavík / Blue Lagoon is geographically contained but can change openings on short notice — verify at booking time.

    The route: four bases, three moves, open-jaw

    Fly into Madrid, out of Florence (or Rome) — no backtracking. The classic published tours squeeze in Seville, Granada, and Venice for 7 bases; that's the pacing trap. This version holds at 4.

    Map unavailable — the numbered stop list below is the route, in order.

      Day by day (14 days)

      1. Days 1–3
        Madrid (3 nights)Arrive day 1 light — jet lag is real at +6 hrs. Prado and Reina Sofía, Retiro Park, a tapas crawl in La Latina. Day trip option: Toledo (30 min by train) only if you're ahead of schedule.
      2. Days 4–6
        Barcelona (3 nights)High-speed train from Madrid. Sagrada Família and Park Güell (timed tickets, booked ahead), Gothic Quarter, Barceloneta for the one beach afternoon this route honestly offers.
      3. Days 7–10
        Rome (4 nights)Fly Barcelona→Rome. Colosseum + Forum, Vatican Museums, Trastevere evenings. Four nights is the forum minimum for Rome — it earns them.
      4. Days 11–13
        Florence (3 nights)90-minute train from Rome. Uffizi and Accademia (timed tickets), Duomo climb, one slow Tuscan evening. Optional Venice day trip is 2 hrs each way — only if you skip something else.
      5. Day 14
        Fly homeFrom Florence (one-stop) or a morning train back to Rome for a wider choice of flights. No backtrack built into the plan either way.

      Flights — cash and points, kept separate

      cash Orlando → Madrid nonstop

      • Iberia nonstop, ~8h 30m–8h 37m. Snapshots found Nov 3 conflict: KAYAK cheapest nonstop $785, typical range $534–$1,012; Priceline's cheapest nonstop in the prior 16 days was $879. Re-check for your dates — treat ~$550–$1,000 as the band.
      • Barcelona→Rome (mid-trip) and Florence/Rome→home are separate one-way tickets in an open-jaw plan; price the whole set, not just the outbound.
      • Tampa: no verified TPA nonstop to Madrid, Rome, or Athens in this research (the TPA Europe document found was from June 2020 — stale). MCO is the gateway.

      points The best points play of the three

      • Chase → Iberia Avios, 1:1. FlyerTalk's consistent advice: Iberia charges very low surcharges on its own flights, which is exactly what makes the Madrid nonstop valuable on points.
      • Avoid British Airways via London for the long haul — forum posters describe BA's surcharges through Heathrow as "insane" and say transferring to Iberia is "where it's at for getting to Europe." (Forum words, FlyerTalk Avios thread.)
      • Avios can move between BA and Iberia accounts if both are 90+ days old and have earned at least 1 Avios.
      • Honest gap: current Iberia award prices couldn't be forum-verified — article figures for off-peak business JFK–Madrid conflict (34k legacy vs ~40.5k on a post-June-2025 chart). Check Iberia.com for your exact date and off-peak status before transferring anything.

      Every leg, every option priced

      Madrid → Barcelona train

      High-speed train 2h30 (a 2026 source notes speed restrictions adding ~25 min — budget ~3h until lifted), advance fares from ~€9–€90, up to ~€150 last-minute; door-to-door ~3h30–4h, city center to city center. Flight is 1h15 in the air but 4h30–5h30 door-to-door, €40–€150 — slower in real life. Bus 7h20–12h, €15–€55 — only if money beats time. Car ~6h, €120–€200 all-in — no reason to.

      Barcelona → Rome flight

      Fly it. The train version is 18–28 hours with 2–3 changes (that's the Rome–Madrid rail reality) — a full day burned. This flight is the trip's hinge: it's the one leg where a delay compresses the Italy half, so book a sane departure time, not the last flight of the day.

      Rome → Florence train

      High-speed train 1h25–1h40, Termini → Santa Maria Novella, both central. From ~€14.90 booked ahead to ~€50–55 near departure; regional trains take 3h40–4h30 for ~€25 and aren't worth it. Car ~3h plus tolls (~€25) and Florence's ZTL camera zones — fines in secondary guides run €80–100+ per gate. Don't drive in Florence.

      Inside the cities

      Metro + walking covers Madrid, Barcelona, and Rome. Rideshare exists (Uber operates in Madrid and Rome; Cabify/FreeNow are the local equivalents to know) but you won't need it daily. In Italy, high-speed trains need seat reservations — included with the ticket; regional trains don't, but validate before boarding. Forums say Eurail passes are generally poor value in Italy; advance Trenitalia/Italo fares beat them.

      What Spain + Italy does badly

      • It's cities back-to-back with no decompression half. By day 10, another cathedral and timed-entry queue can feel like work. There is no slow section unless you build one.
      • Summer heat is the failure mode: inland Spain and Rome/Florence hit 95–100°F+ in July–August, plus Ferragosto closures around Aug 15 in Italy. May and Sep–early Oct are the sweet spots (Madrid/Barcelona highs ~71–82°F in shoulder season).
      • The Andalusia temptation: Seville and Granada are superb — and adding them makes it 6–7 bases with a second Spanish rail region. That's a different (also good) trip; it doesn't fit inside this one.
      • Two languages, two rail systems, one mid-trip flight. Manageable, but it's the most "systems" of the Mediterranean options.

      The route: one island only, Athens last

      Florence → Rome → Athens → Santorini → Athens buffer → home. Forums repeat two rules for Greece: stay inside one island group, and do Athens last so an island delay can't strand your flight home. The classic 6-base version (adding Venice and Mykonos) leaves ≤2 nights everywhere — this version refuses it.

      Map unavailable — the numbered stop list below is the route, in order.

        Day by day (14 days)

        1. Days 1–3
          Florence (3 nights)Arrive into Italy (one-stop from Florida). Uffizi, Accademia, Duomo — timed tickets booked ahead. Starting in Florence instead of Rome keeps the biggest city for when the jet lag (+6 hrs) has worn off.
        2. Days 4–7
          Rome (4 nights)90-minute train south. Colosseum, Vatican, Trastevere. The museum-heavy half of the trip happens here, first, on purpose.
        3. Days 8–9
          Athens (2 nights)Fly Rome→Athens. Acropolis early morning, Acropolis Museum, Plaka evenings. Two nights is enough for the core — that's the honest read.
        4. Days 10–12
          Santorini (3 nights)Fly down (don't ferry — see legs below). Oia and Fira, a caldera boat trip, one beach day (Kamari/Perissa), sunsets. The slow half of the trip.
        5. Day 13
          Athens buffer nightBack to Athens a full day before flying home. Non-negotiable: island flights and ferries get cancelled in wind, and a same-day island→transatlantic connection is how trips end badly.
        6. Day 14
          Fly home from AthensOne-stop back to Florida, typically via a European or US hub.

        Flights — cash and points, kept separate

        cash Getting there and back

        • No verified nonstop from MCO or TPA to Rome or Athens was found in this research — plan on one stop (via a US hub or a European gateway like Madrid, Frankfurt, or London).
        • Honest gap: no trustworthy cash snapshot for Florida→Rome/Athens was sourced in this pass the way Madrid and Keflavík were. Don't budget this option off a number that isn't here — it needs a date-specific check.
        • Rome→Athens mid-trip: ~2 hrs in the air, budget carriers cited €30–€80 advance in one guide, €45–€200 in another, legacy €100–€250. Wide range = book it early, and count 6–8 hrs door-to-door.

        points More programs, one trap

        • Chase transfers 1:1 to United, Air Canada Aeroplan, Air France/KLM Flying Blue, and Virgin Atlantic — all can price Italy/Greece routings. The route exists; the question is the cash fees on top.
        • The surcharge trap (FlyerTalk, Aeroplan thread): United charges no carrier surcharges on awards; Aeroplan does, depending on the operating airline — Air Canada, Lufthansa, Austrian, Brussels attract them; United, Swiss, Turkish didn't in that discussion. The same seat can cost very different cash via different programs. Always compare the full cash total, not just the mileage.
        • One article (not forum-verified) claims Aeroplan's North Atlantic partner business price rose 60k → 78k on Apr 1, 2026. Re-check live before planning around any Aeroplan number.

        Every leg, every option priced

        Florence → Rome train

        Same as the Spain + Italy route: high-speed train 1h25–1h40, from ~€14.90 advance to ~€50–55 late. The Italy half of this trip is just as rail-easy.

        Rome → Athens flight the structural break

        There is no train across the Adriatic. Flight: ~2h air, 6–8h door-to-door (see prices above). The alternative — train to Bari (4h15), overnight ferry to Patras (16–18h), then bus/train to Athens (3–3h30) — totals 24–30 hours. It's an adventure, not a transfer; on a 14-day trip it's a day and a half gone. Fly.

        Athens → Santorini flight

        Flight 45–55 min in the air, 3–4h door-to-door, ~€40 low season to €150+ peak (baggage fees can flip the comparison). High-speed ferry ~5 hrs crossing (6–7h door-to-door), ~€60–€110 in one source's range, €45–€90 in another; conventional ferry 7.5–9 hrs from ~€46. Forum color: conventional Blue Star boats are bigger, steadier, with decks and caldera views; SeaJets fast boats are pricier, smaller, less stable. If you're prone to seasickness, the flight wins twice. Winter warning: high-speed sailings thin to almost nothing Nov–Mar; the flight keeps running.

        Inside Greece

        Athens: metro + walking; don't rent a car for the city itself. Islands: local buses and taxis; rideshare apps aren't the system here the way Grab was in Vietnam. English is widely spoken and road signs are bilingual (Greek + phonetic English) per forum posters — Greece is the lowest-language-friction country on this page after Iceland.

        What Italy + Greece does badly

        • Logistics are the messiest of the three. No Greek rail equivalent, ports and island transfers, and a forced backtrack through Athens to get home. Every island move is weather-dependent.
        • Most season-sensitive option. July–August: 95°F+ heat, double-priced Santorini/Mykonos hotels, meltemi cancellations, and Greece has the most peak-concentrated tourism of the three (72.7% of activity May–Sep, per one industry study). November–March: island hotels close and ferries thin.
        • Santorini's price and crowds can dominate the whole budget in peak season. Naxos and Paros are the calmer, cheaper forum-favorite alternatives — but they're not the postcard, and swapping them changes what the trip promises.
        • The jet lag is the deepest (+7 hrs in Greece) and the home-bound routing is the least direct of the three.

        What forums actually say about Chase points for these routes

        Sourced from FlyerTalk and Rick Steves forum threads that were opened and read on Nov 3, 2026. Where a number comes from an article or award-search tool instead of a forum, it says so — no forum price was invented, and some things forums simply haven't verified are listed as gaps at the bottom.

        Your balances (on file)
        Chase ~150k · Capital One ~110k — re-verify in your accounts before planning around them
        The golden rule
        Find the exact seat first, transfer the exact amount last. Transfers are effectively one-way.
        Who can transfer
        Only premium cards (Sapphire Preferred/Reserve, Ink Preferred). Freedom-family points must be combined into a premium account first.
        Transfer speed
        Usually instant for BA, Virgin, United; Aeroplan is variable — older reports run 30 hrs to 72–96 hrs. A seat can vanish during a slow transfer.

        Route by route

        Madrid — the sweet spot strongest play

        Chase → Iberia Avios 1:1 for the Orlando–Madrid nonstop. FlyerTalk's Avios thread: Iberia has "very low surcharges on its flights," while BA long-haul via London gets "dented by high surcharges" — posters called BA's "insane" and said Iberia is "where it's at for getting to Europe." Move Avios BA↔Iberia only if both accounts are 90+ days old with ≥1 Avios earned. Not verified: today's exact award price — article figures for off-peak business conflict (34k legacy vs ~40.5k post-June-2025 chart, peak ~50–51k). Price your date on Iberia.com first.

        Rome & Athens — compare the cash fees, not the miles

        Chase → United, Aeroplan, Flying Blue, or Virgin Atlantic. FlyerTalk's Aeroplan thread is the key reading: United adds no carrier surcharges on awards; Aeroplan adds them per operating carrier (Air Canada, Lufthansa, Austrian, Brussels = surcharges; United, Swiss, Turkish = none, in that discussion). A lower-mileage Aeroplan booking on a surcharge carrier can cost more cash than the same seat via United. No forum-verified current price for TPA/MCO–Rome or –Athens exists yet — this needs a live search once dates exist.

        Reykjavík — the workaround route

        No direct Chase → Icelandair path (Saga Club doesn't take US transferable points, per award-tool sources). The detours: Chase → JetBlue (1:1) for Icelandair economy — a tool figure of 17,000 pts + ~$102 one-way Boston–Keflavík is a lead to verify, not a Florida price; Chase → Virgin Atlantic for Delta's seasonal Reykjavík flights, article-quoted at 30,000–50,000 pts round-trip economy. No FlyerTalk thread found on a TPA/MCO–Keflavík award sweet spot at all. Cash may honestly win this route — the nonstop's cash band ($550–$950) is low enough that burning transferable points needs a real comparison first.

        Worst-value traps the forums name

        • BA via London on Avios — surcharges eat the value; route through Iberia instead.
        • Transferring before the seat is confirmed — the single most repeated mistake. Points move one way; seats don't wait.
        • Judging by mileage alone — dynamic programs move miles with cash price; surcharges move cash the other way. Compare total cost: points + all fees vs. the cash fare.
        • Portal redemptions — article sources put Chase portal value around ~1¢/point, below good transfer sweet spots (article figure, not forum-verified).
        • Peak-date awards — forums' logic: don't burn points on a peak date just because you have them; sometimes the cash fare is the better deal (articles noted Iberia cash business fares that beat peak awards).

        Capital One, briefly

        Your ~110k Capital One miles are a second, separate pool — this research pass focused on Chase because you asked about Chase. Capital One transfers to many of the same programs (Flying Blue, Aeroplan, Virgin, BA/Iberia Avios among them), so the same plays mostly work from either pool — but no Capital One–specific pricing was verified in this pass, and the pools can't be combined into one program balance except by transferring both into the same airline account.

        Plainly not verified — don't plan on these yet

        • No direct Reddit threads (r/awardtravel, r/travel) for TPA/MCO → Madrid/Rome/Athens/Keflavík were found in this pass despite site-specific searches — so nothing here is dressed up as Reddit wisdom. The forum record is FlyerTalk + Rick Steves.
        • A claimed 30% Chase → BA/Iberia/Aer Lingus transfer bonus ending Dec 1, 2026 is article-only — check inside your Chase account; if real, it changes the Madrid math and has a deadline.
        • The Aeroplan 60k → 78k partner-price change, the JetBlue 17k Keflavík figure, and the Virgin/Delta Reykjavík range are all article/tool claims awaiting live verification.
        • Every award price needs a live seat check on the airline's own site for your actual dates before any transfer. Nothing has been transferred, and nothing should be on research alone.

        Season decides more than country does

        Jet lag, from the sleep research

        Eastbound is the harder direction. A 2025 study from NUS Medicine's Centre for Sleep and Cognition with ŌURA — 1.5 million nights across 60,000+ trips — found sleep duration typically recovers in ~2 days, but sleep timing and structure can take over a week to realign, with eastward travel and more time zones making it worse. A commonly cited CDC rule of thumb (via secondary summary) is ~1 day of adjustment per time zone eastbound.

        DestinationHours ahead of FloridaWhat that means for a 14-day trip
        Iceland+4–5Lightest hit — day 1 is usable, day 2 is close to normal
        Spain / Italy+6Keep day 1 in the arrival city light; full energy by day 3–4
        Greece+7Deepest shift — one more reason the Italy + Greece plan front-loads Florence, not the biggest sights

        US and EU daylight-saving changeovers fall on different weeks in March and October, so the gap can shift by an hour around those dates — check against your actual travel dates.

        Cost per day — why the sources argue

        There's no single authoritative daily-cost figure; guides include different things. Two published guide sets (solo, excluding the flight to Europe):

        CountryBudget / dayMid-range / day
        Iceland$130–180$250–320
        Italy$70–100$140–180
        Spain$60–90$130–160
        Greece$50–80$120–150

        What's robust across every source: Iceland is the most expensive, Spain the cheapest (or tied) of the Mediterranean three, and high season inflates accommodation roughly 30–50%. A 2026 Hellosafe survey model disagrees on Greece (pricier than Italy in its island-heavy basket) — one more reason Santorini specifically breaks the "Greece is cheap" rule.
